claim: Ichthyosporeans are the only known lineage besides animals that forms coenocytes during their life cycles among holozoans.
source: Among holozoans — a clade that includes animals and their closest unicellular relatives (Figure 1A) — ichthyosporeans are the only known lineage besides animals that forms coenocytes during their life cycles (Mendoza et al., 2002; de Mendoza et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mendoza et al., 2002 and de Mendoza et al., 2015

claim: All characterized ichthyosporeans proliferate through rounds of nuclear divisions within a cell-walled coenocyte, followed by release of newborn cells.
source: All characterized ichthyosporeans proliferate through rounds of nuclear divisions within a cell-walled coenocyte, followed by release of newborn cells (Marshall and Berbee, 2011; Marshall and Berbee, 2013; Suga and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013; Whisler, 1968).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Marshall and Berbee, 2011; Marshall and Berbee, 2013; Suga and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013; Whisler, 1968

claim: Individual coenocytes of S. arctica exhibit growth in cell size until approximately 60 hr, after which they undergo release of newborn cells.
source: Individual coenocytes exhibit growth in cell size until approximately 60 hr, after which they undergo release of newborn cells (Figure 1B, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1

claim: Prior to cell release, the coenocytes darken along the periphery, and the dark front begins to advance towards the center.
source: Time-lapse imaging revealed that prior to cell release, the coenocytes darken along the periphery, and the dark front begins to advance towards the center (Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Video 2

claim: An abrupt internal morphological change termed 'flip' occurs in the coenocyte when the dark front disappears.
source: Afterwards, we observed an abrupt internal morphological change in the coenocyte, when the front disappears. We termed this event 'flip' (Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations in Video 2

claim: The flip occurred in all the coenocytes and can be reliably detected on kymographs.
source: The flip occurred in all the coenocytes and can be reliably detected on kymographs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Coenocytes stop growing approximately 9 hr before the flip.
source: Aligning individual coenocyte size traces to this specific common temporal marker, we observe that coenocytes stop growing approximately 9 hr before the flip (Figure 1D and E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Growth and cellularization are temporally separated stages of the coenocytic cycle of S. arctica.
source: This shows that the growth stage and cellularization are temporally separated.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that coenocytes stop growing approximately 9 hr before the flip

claim: The cellularization can be divided into a temporally less variable pre-flip phase (~9 hr) and a variable post-flip phase.
source: The cellularization can be divided into a temporally less variable pre-flip phase (~9 hr) and a variable post-flip phase (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: A rapid increase in FM4-64 intensity at the periphery of the coenocyte occurs 30 min prior to flip.
source: We observed a rapid increase in FM4-64 intensity at the periphery of the coenocyte 30 min prior to flip (Figure 2A, panel II, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, panel II, Videos 3 and 4

claim: Plasma membrane invagination sites formed at the periphery and progressed synchronously from the outside toward the center of the coenocyte, forming polarized, polyhedral cells.
source: The plasma membrane invagination sites formed at the periphery and progressed synchronously from the outside toward the center of the coenocyte, forming polarized, polyhedral cells (Figure 2A, panels II-V, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, panels II-V, Videos 3 and 4

claim: During the first 10–15 min, the invaginations advance at a rate of about 0.3 µm/min.
source: During the first 10–15 min, the invaginations advance at a rate of about 0,3 µm/min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The slow phase of membrane invagination is followed by a rapid phase where membrane invaginates at a rate of about 0.9 µm/min leading to flip.
source: This period is followed by a rapid phase where membrane invaginates at a rate of about 0,9 µm/min leading to flip (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Following flip, cells lost their polyhedral shape and became round, suggesting that they were no longer attached to each other.
source: Finally, following flip, cells lost their polyhedral shape and became round, suggesting that they were no longer attached to each other (Figure 2A, panel VI, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, panel VI, Videos 3 and 4, with inference about cell attachment

claim: During growth, actin localized exclusively as small patches at the surface of the coenocyte.
source: During growth, actin localized exclusively as small patches at the surface of the coenocyte (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panel I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panel I

claim: At the onset of cellularization, multiple actin patches increased in size to form actin nodes.
source: Only at the onset of cellularization, multiple actin patches increased in size to form actin nodes (Figure 2B, panel I and II, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panel II).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, panels I and II, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panel II

claim: Cortical compartmentalization surrounding the nuclei occurs through gradual formation of an actin filament network solely at the cortex of the coenocyte.
source: This phase was followed by cortical compartmentalization surrounding the nuclei through gradual formation of an actin filament network solely at the cortex of the coenocyte (Figure 2B, panel III, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panels III and IV).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, panel III, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panels III and IV

claim: A layer of cells was transiently formed by inward growth of the actin filaments from the cortex.
source: Following this cortical compartmentalization, a layer of cells was transiently formed by inward growth of the actin filaments from the cortex (Figure 2B, panels IV and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panels V and VI).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, panel IV and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, panels V and VI

claim: During the polarized cell layer formation stage, the actin signal intensity was uneven and higher on the internal side, and nuclei were localized close to the cortex, indicating that cells are polarized.
source: During this stage, the actin signal intensity was uneven and higher on the internal side (Video 5), and nuclei were localized close to the cortex, indicating that cells are polarized (Figure 2B, panel IV, Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, panel IV and Video 5

claim: The cortical actin network formed prior to the appearance of the membrane dye.
source: We found that the cortical actin network formed prior to the appearance of the membrane dye (Figure 2C, panel II).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, panel II

claim: The intensity of FM4-64FX labeling increased and co-localized with the underlying actin network around the time of plasma membrane invagination.
source: The intensity of FM4-64FX labeling also increased and co-localized with the underlying actin network around the time of plasma membrane invagination (Figure 2C, panels III and IV).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, panels III and IV

claim: The cortical actin network determines the site of plasma membrane invagination.
source: This suggests that the cortical actin network determines the site of plasma membrane invagination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the cortical actin network formed prior to membrane invagination and co-localized with it

claim: Cell wall formation occurs in the post-flip stage, with labeling co-localizing with the membrane marker FM4-64FX around individual cells.
source: Finally, to determine the timing of cell wall formation, we stained the cells with calcofluor. We observed that labeling co-localized with the membrane marker FM4-64FX around individual cells in the post-flip stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Newborn cells build the cell wall before release.
source: This shows that the newborn cells already build the cell wall before the release, as was suggested previously in other Sphaeroforma species (Marshall and Berbee, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from calcofluor staining and a citation to Marshall and Berbee, 2013

claim: The re-sequenced genome assembly of S. arctica comprised 142,721,209 bp with greatly improved metrics compared to the previous assembly.
source: The final assembly sequences comprised 142,721,209 bp, and the metrics were greatly improved compared to the previous assembly (Grau-Bové et al., 2017) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome assembly data and comparison to Grau-Bové et al., 2017

claim: 33,682 protein coding genes and 1071 lincRNAs were predicted in the S. arctica genome.
source: In total, 33,682 protein coding genes and 1071 lincRNAs were predicted using this combined pipeline (see Materilas and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome annotation data

claim: Clustering of transcript abundance data revealed a clear separation between the transcriptomes of the growth stage (12 hr to 42 hr time points) and the cellularization stage (48 hr to 66 hr time points).
source: Clustering of transcript abundance data from both biological replicates revealed a clear separation between the transcriptomes of the growth stage (12 hr to 42 hr time points) and the cellularization stage (48 hr to 66 hr time points) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Consensus clustering extracted 9 clusters of co-expressed transcripts with a total of 4441 protein coding genes.
source: Among the expressed transcripts (defined as mean expression levels higher than 0.5 tpm across all samples; in total 13,542 coding genes and 1015 lincRNAs), consensus clustering using Clust (Abu-Jamous and Kelly, 2018) extracted 9 clusters of co-expressed transcripts with a total of 4441 protein coding genes (Figure 3B), while the rest of the transcripts were not assigned to any co-expression cluster.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3B and citation to Abu-Jamous and Kelly, 2018

claim: Three main clusters of genes are sharply activated during cellularization (clusters 5, 6 and 7), which contain transcripts expressed at early, mid and late cellularization, respectively.
source: Among the cellularization clusters, we obtain three main clusters of genes sharply activated during cellularization (clusters 5, 6 and 7), which contain transcripts expressed at early, mid and late cellularization, respectively (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3B and D

claim: Cellularization is associated with extensive sharp transcriptional activation in multiple temporal waves, affecting 17% of the expressed transcriptome.
source: Altogether, this shows that cellularization is associated with extensive sharp transcriptional activation in multiple temporal waves, in total affecting 17% of the expressed transcriptome.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the clustering analysis showing multiple cellularization clusters

claim: 2022 genes are affected by intron retention (12.9% of all intron-bearing genes, totaling 4310 introns).
source: This analysis identified 2022 genes affected by intron retention (12.9% of all intron-bearing genes, totaling 4310 introns), 914 by exon skipping (12.3% of genes with >2 exons, 1206 exons) and 44 with mutually exclusive exons (0.7% of genes with >3 exons, involving 118 exon pairs) in all samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by alternative splicing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: 914 genes are affected by exon skipping (12.3% of genes with >2 exons, 1206 exons).
source: This analysis identified 2022 genes affected by intron retention (12.9% of all intron-bearing genes, totaling 4310 introns), 914 by exon skipping (12.3% of genes with >2 exons, 1206 exons) and 44 with mutually exclusive exons (0.7% of genes with >3 exons, involving 118 exon pairs) in all samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by alternative splicing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: 44 genes have mutually exclusive exons (0.7% of genes with >3 exons, involving 118 exon pairs).
source: This analysis identified 2022 genes affected by intron retention (12.9% of all intron-bearing genes, totaling 4310 introns), 914 by exon skipping (12.3% of genes with >2 exons, 1206 exons) and 44 with mutually exclusive exons (0.7% of genes with >3 exons, involving 118 exon pairs) in all samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by alternative splicing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: Skipped exons were more likely to be in-frame (38.63%, compared to 30.33% of in-frame exons in genes with >2 exons, p=4.34e-05, Fisher's exact test).
source: Interestingly, skipped exons were more likely to be in-frame (38.63%, compared to 30.33% of in-frame exons in genes with >2 exons, p=4.34e-05, Fisher's exact test) and yield non-truncated transcripts, a phenomenon commonly observed in animal transcriptomes but not in transcriptomes of other unicellular eukaryotes (Grau-Bové et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and citation to Grau-Bové et al., 2018

claim: Alternative splicing likely does not play a major role in regulation of the coenocytic cycle and cellularization of S. arctica.
source: Overall, although pervasive, alternative splicing likely does not play a major role in regulation of the coenocytic cycle and cellularization of S. arctica.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AS events do not vary dramatically along the growth cycle

claim: LincRNAs represent ~3% of total transcript abundance across the time series.
source: Overall, lincRNAs represent ~3% of total transcript abundance across the time series (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: 70 lincRNA transcripts clustered with coding genes into temporally co-expressed clusters.
source: Among the long non-coding RNAs, 70 lincRNA transcripts clustered with coding genes into temporally co-expressed clusters (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: 24 of the S. arctica lncRNAs were conserved in distantly related ichthyosporean species such as Creolimax fragrantissima, Pirum gemmata and Abeoforma whisleri.
source: Sequence homology searches revealed that 24 of the S. arctica lncRNAs were conserved in distantly related ichthyosporean species such as Creolimax fragrantissima, Pirum gemmata and Abeoforma whisleri (estimated to have diverged ~500 million years ago; Parfrey et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence homology searches and citation to Parfrey et al., 2011

claim: The conservation of lincRNAs in ichthyosporeans represents a remarkable depth of conservation, since animal lincRNAs are not conserved between animal phyla.
source: This is a remarkable depth of conservation, since animal lincRNAs are not conserved between animal phyla (Bråte et al., 2015; Gaiti et al., 2015; Hezroni et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bråte et al., 2015; Gaiti et al., 2015; Hezroni et al., 2015

claim: Conserved lincRNAs were on average longer than non-conserved ones.
source: However, we found that conserved lincRNAs were on average longer than non-conserved ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and, strikingly, expressed at much higher levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Figure 4B

claim: Conserved lincRNAs were expressed at much higher levels than non-conserved ones.
source: However, we found that conserved lincRNAs were on average longer than non-conserved ones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and, strikingly, expressed at much higher levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Among the 24 deeply conserved lincRNAs, five clustered in the temporally co-expressed clusters, which is higher than expected by chance (p=0.0166, Fisher's exact test).
source: Among the 24 deeply conserved lincRNAs, five clustered in the temporally co-expressed clusters, which is higher than expected by chance (p=0.0166, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis

claim: Three deeply conserved lincRNAs belonged to the cellularization clusters.
source: Among these, three belonged to the cellularization clusters, including, lincRNA asmbl_31839, which has a remarkably high sequence similarity with its homologs from other ichthyosporeans (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis and sequence similarity data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: The transcriptional regulation of lincRNA asmbl_31839 is independent of the transcriptional regulation of its neighboring coding genes (located within 3 kb).
source: Furthermore, its transcriptional regulation is independent of the transcriptional regulation of its neighboring coding genes (located within 3 kb) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Younger genes show a trend toward more variable expression throughout the coenocytic cycle.
source: Analysis of gene expression by phylostrata revealed a trend toward more variable expression throughout the coenocytic cycle in younger genes (Figure 4E), although their mean expression levels were lower (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylostratigraphic analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Growth clusters are enriched for pan-eukaryotic genes.
source: Analysis of enrichment of gene phylostrata in each gene expression cluster (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) showed that the growth clusters are enriched for pan-eukaryotic genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylostratigraphic enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: Cellularization clusters were enriched for younger genes.
source: In contrast, we find that the cellularization clusters were enriched for younger genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylostratigraphic enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C

claim: Genes with ichthyosporean origins were significantly enriched in all three of the largest cellularization clusters.
source: Importantly, we found that genes with ichthyosporean origins were significantly enriched in all three of the largest cellularization clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylostratigraphic enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C

claim: The transcriptome age index reveals a statistically significant hourglass pattern (p=4.4 * 10−5 and p=0.02 for replicates 1 and 2, Reductive Hourglass test), with older genes expressed at later stages of growth, and younger genes expressed during early growth and cellularization.
source: Finally, computing the transcriptome age index (Domazet-Lošo and Tautz, 2010) to assess the overall age of the transcriptome across the life cycle revealed a statistically significant hourglass pattern (p=4.4 * 10−5 and p=0.02 for replicates 1 and 2, Reductive Hourglass test; Drost et al., 2015), with older genes expressed at later stages of growth, and younger genes expressed during early growth and cellularization (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome age index analysis shown in Figure 4F and citations to Domazet-Lošo and Tautz, 2010 and Drost et al., 2015

claim: Cellularization is a comparatively younger process, whereas the growth stage represents an evolutionarily ancient process.
source: Altogether, the phylostratigraphic analysis suggests that cellularization is a comparatively younger process, whereas the growth stage represent an evolutionarily ancient process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phylostratigraphic analysis showing enrichment of younger genes in cellularization clusters

claim: The largest growth cluster (cluster 1) was enriched in GO terms related to cell growth and biosynthesis.
source: The largest growth cluster (cluster 1) was enriched in GO terms related to cell growth and biosynthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: Early and mid-cellularization clusters 5 and 6 were enriched for GO terms related to membrane organization and actin cytoskeleton.
source: Early and mid-cellularization clusters 5 and 6 were enriched for GO terms related to membrane organization and actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: Late cellularization clusters were enriched for GO terms related to actin, cell adhesion and polarity.
source: Late cellularization clusters were, in addition to GO terms related to actin, also enriched for GO terms related to cell adhesion and polarity.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: In Drosophila blastoderm, cellularization is regulated by several zygotically transcribed genes and relies on extensive membrane trafficking controlled by Rab GTPases.
source: In the Drosophila blastoderm, cellularization is regulated by several zygotically transcribed genes (Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002) and relies on extensive membrane trafficking controlled by Rab GTPases (Bucci et al., 1992; Dollar et al., 2002; Pelissier et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002; Bucci et al., 1992; Dollar et al., 2002; Pelissier et al., 2003

claim: No homologs of any Drosophila zygotically transcribed genes known to regulate cellularization were found in S. arctica.
source: In S. arctica, we did not find homologs of any Drosophila zygotically transcribed genes known to regulate cellularization (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by homology search results

claim: The expression of homologs of Rab5 and Rab11 as well as tubulins and kinesins, except for one (S. arctica Kinesin 2), is constant throughout the coenocytic cycle.
source: However, we found that the expression of homologs of Rab5 and Rab11 as well as tubulins and kinesins, except for one (S. arctica Kinesin 2), is constant throughout the coenocytic cycle (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5A, B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: All actin nucleators of the formin family and members of the Arp2/3 complex peaked during cellularization.
source: On the other hand, we found many actin-associated genes dynamically expressed. All actin nucleators of the formin family and members of the Arp2/3 complex peaked during cellularization (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Formins exhibited sharp expression peaks, whereas the gene expression of the Arp2/3 complex was initiated earlier and increased gradually.
source: In contrast to formins, which largely exhibited sharp peaks, the gene expression of the Arp2/3 complex was initiated earlier and increased gradually (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Septins, cofilin, profilin and myosin V were temporally co-expressed during mid-cellularization and peaked at the same time as actin nucleators.
source: Septins, cofilin, profilin and myosin V were temporally co-expressed during mid-cellularization and peaked at the same time as actin nucleators (Figure 5D), whereas myosin II, which has a role in organizing actin filaments and contractility, peaked later (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Myosin II peaked later than septins, cofilin, profilin and myosin V.
source: Septins, cofilin, profilin and myosin V were temporally co-expressed during mid-cellularization and peaked at the same time as actin nucleators (Figure 5D), whereas myosin II, which has a role in organizing actin filaments and contractility, peaked later (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The expression of three out of four members of the Cdc42/Rho1 orthogroup was sharply activated during late cellularization.
source: We likewise found the expression of three out of four members of the Cdc42/Rho1 orthogroup to be sharply activated during late cellularization (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Both integrin receptors, alpha and beta, as well as all cytoplasmic members of the integrin adhesome, are temporally co-expressed during late cellularization in S. arctica.
source: We observed that in S. arctica, both integrin receptors, alpha and beta, as well as all cytoplasmic members, are temporally co-expressed during late cellularization (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The expression of two out of three Aardvark transcripts, as well as the expression of the alpha catenin homolog, peaked during late cellularization.
source: We found that the expression of two out of three Aardvark transcripts, as well as the expression of the alpha catenin homolog, peaked during late cellularization (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Both cell-matrix and cell-cell adhesion pathways, largely conserved between animals and ichthyosporeans, play a role in the establishment of the polarized layer of cells during late cellularization.
source: This suggests that both cell-matrix and cell-cell adhesion pathways, largely conserved between animals and ichthyosporeans, play a role in the establishment of the polarized layer of cells during late cellularization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal co-expression of integrin and catenin genes during late cellularization

claim: Microtubule inhibition did not prevent plasma membrane invagination, although it resulted in a delay of flip and release of newborn cells.
source: Microtubule inhibition did not prevent plasma membrane invagination, although it resulted in a delay of flip and release of newborn cells (Figure 6A and B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7

claim: MBC treatment caused a loss of the uniform spacing of the nuclei and actin filaments during the cortical compartmentalization stage of cellularization.
source: Furthermore, by staining the MBC-treated cells with DAPI and phalloidin, we observed a loss of the uniform spacing of the nuclei and actin filaments during the cortical compartmentalization stage of cellularization (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6C

claim: After MBC treatment, newborn cells varied in size and number of nuclei.
source: After MBC treatment, newborn cells varied in size and number of nuclei (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C, Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C, and Video 6

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton is not essential for plasma membrane invagination but is crucial for nucleus and actin filament positioning at the cortex of the coenocyte.
source: These results suggest that the microtubule cytoskeleton is not essential for plasma membrane invagination but is crucial for nucleus and actin filament positioning at the cortex of the coenocyte.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MBC treatment results

claim: Cells treated with Latrunculin A lacked any actin patches or actin filaments and failed to undergo flip or produce newborn cells.
source: Cells treated with Latrunculin A lacked any actin patches or actin filaments and failed to undergo flip or produce newborn cells (Figure 6A-C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6A-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7

claim: Plasma membrane invagination did not occur after LatA treatment.
source: Furthermore, plasma membrane invagination did not occur after LatA treatment (Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Videos 6 and 7

claim: CK666-treated cells formed cortical actin patches, but were not able to form actin nodes, and they were unable to generate plasma membrane invaginations.
source: In contrast, CK666-treated cells formed cortical actin patches, but were not able to form actin nodes, and they were unable to generate plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 6A–6C, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6A-C, Videos 6 and 7

claim: The actin cytoskeleton and Arp2/3-mediated actin nucleation are required for the formation of actin nodes, the first step in the cellularization of S. arctica.
source: These results show that the actin cytoskeleton and Arp2/3-mediated actin nucleation are required for the formation of actin nodes, the first step in the cellularization of S. arctica.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the LatA and CK666 treatment results

claim: The formin inhibitor SMIFH2 did not block the formation of actin nodes, but it prevented the formation of actin filaments in the later stages.
source: In contrast, the formin inhibitor SMIFH2 did not block the formation of actin nodes, but it prevented the formation of actin filaments in the later stages (Figure 6A–6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6A-C

claim: Plasma membrane invagination did not occur after SMIFH2 treatment.
source: In addition, the plasma membrane invagination did not occur (Figure 6A-C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7), although we note that a small fraction of cells was not affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6A-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7

claim: Formins play a role in the nucleation of actin filaments after the formation of actin nodes.
source: This suggests that formins play a role in the nucleation of actin filaments after the formation of actin nodes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the SMIFH2 treatment results

claim: Blebbistatin treatment blocked plasma membrane invaginations and prevented cellularization.
source: Finally, we assessed the role of Myosin II, using blebbistatin, an inhibitor of Myosin II ATPase activity (Kovács et al., 2004). Blebbistatin treatment blocked plasma membrane invaginations and prevented cellularization (Figure 6A-C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6A-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Videos 6 and 7, and citation to Kovács et al., 2004

claim: In coenocytes where plasma membrane invaginations started but the cell layer was not yet formed, a retraction of already present invaginations was observed when treated with blebbistatin.
source: In coenocytes where plasma membrane invaginations started but the cell layer was not yet formed, we observed a retraction of already present invaginations when treated with blebbistatin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Video 8

claim: In coenocytes where the cell layer was formed but polarized growth was not complete, blebbistatin treatment prevented polarized growth but allowed the release of cells of different cell sizes.
source: Additionally, in coenocytes where the cell layer was formed but polarized growth was not complete, blebbistatin treatment prevented polarized growth but allowed the release of cells of different cell sizes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and Video 8

claim: Blebbistatin-treated cells were able to form actin filaments, but they had an aberrant wavy cortical actin filament network, suggesting that inhibition of Myosin II causes loss of actin crosslinking and actin network contractility.
source: Although blebbistatin-treated cells were able to form actin filaments, they had an aberrant wavy cortical actin filament network, suggesting that inhibition of Myosin II causes loss of actin crosslinking and actin network contractility (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6C, with inference about the mechanism

claim: The actomyosin apparatus is essential for cellularization in S. arctica.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the actomyosin apparatus is essential for cellularization in S. arctica and reveal a temporal sequence of involvement of Arp2/3 complex, formins and Myosin II (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pharmacological inhibition experiments

claim: There is a temporal sequence of involvement of Arp2/3 complex, formins and Myosin II in cellularization.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the actomyosin apparatus is essential for cellularization in S. arctica and reveal a temporal sequence of involvement of Arp2/3 complex, formins and Myosin II (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments and shown in Figure 6D

claim: The temporal sequence of Arp2/3, formins and myosin II involvement is reflected in the relative timing of expression of Arp2/3, formins and myosin II genes.
source: This temporal sequence is reflected in the relative timing of expression of Arp2/3, formins and myosin II genes (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: At the onset of cellularization, Arp2/3 complex mediates the formation of actin nodes at the cortex of the coenocyte.
source: We show that at the onset of cellularization, Arp2/3 complex mediates the formation of actin nodes at the cortex of the coenocyte.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments and imaging data

claim: Formin-dependent nucleation of actin filaments follows the formation of actin nodes.
source: This is followed by formin-dependent nucleation of actin filaments.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments

claim: Actin filaments are crosslinked in a Myosin II-dependent manner, which results in formation of a cortical actomyosin network that surrounds evenly spaced nuclei.
source: These actin filaments are then crosslinked in a Myosin II-dependent manner, which results in formation of a cortical actomyosin network that surrounds evenly spaced nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments and imaging data

claim: The spatial organization of both the actomyosin network and nuclei depends on microtubules.
source: This spatial organization of both the actomyosin network and nuclei depends on microtubules.
evidence: The claim is supported by MBC treatment experiments

claim: The localization of the actomyosin network determines the sites of plasma membrane invaginations and drives their inward growth through a slow and a fast phase, resulting in the formation of a polarized layer of cells.
source: The localization of the actomyosin network determines the sites of plasma membrane invaginations and drives their inward growth through a slow and a fast phase, resulting in the formation of a polarized layer of cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data and pharmacological inhibition experiments

claim: The polarized cell layer formation stage co-occurs with transcriptional activation of genes involved in cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion.
source: This stage co-occurs with transcriptional activation of genes involved in cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data

claim: Polarized growth persists until the internal cavity is occupied, after which the polyhedrally-shaped cells undergo flip, lose polarization and detach from each other.
source: Polarized growth persists until the internal cavity is occupied, after which the polyhedrally-shaped cells undergo flip, lose polarization and detach from each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data

claim: Future newborn cells form the cell wall before they are released and initiate a new coenocytic cycle.
source: At this point, future newborn cells form the cell wall before they are released and initiate a new coenocytic cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcofluor staining data

claim: The cellularization of S. arctica morphologically resembles the cellularization of the Drosophila blastoderm and shares a common actomyosin pathway for cellularization.
source: Overall, our results show that the cellularization of S. arctica morphologically resembles the cellularization of the Drosophila blastoderm and share a common actomyosin pathway for cellularization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of S. arctica cellularization with Drosophila cellularization

claim: The common ancestor of opisthokonts already had a coenocytic life cycle.
source: First, given the widespread presence of coenocytes in opisthokonts, we have suggested that the common ancestor of opisthokonts already had a coenocytic life cycle (Ondracka et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ondracka et al., 2018

claim: If the common ancestor of opisthokonts had a coenocytic life cycle, cellularization of the coenocyte by the conserved actomyosin mechanism would have already been present in this common ancestor.
source: In this scenario, cellularization of the coenocyte by this conserved actomyosin mechanism would have already been present in this common ancestor.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the hypothesis that the common ancestor had a coenocytic life cycle

claim: In an alternative scenario, coenocytes in animals and ichthyosporeans would have evolved independently, but adopted the same conserved actomyosin mechanism for cellularization.
source: In the second scenario, coenocytes in animals and ichthyosporeans would have evolved independently, but adopted the same conserved actomyosin mechanism for cellularization.
evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative evolutionary scenario

claim: Many genes expressed during cellularization of S. arctica emerged at the onset of ichthyosporeans.
source: Interestingly, we show that many genes expressed during cellularization of S. arctica emerged at the onset of ichthyosporeans.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylostratigraphic analysis

claim: The general mechanisms of cellularization in S. arctica are likely conserved within ichthyosporeans.
source: This strongly suggests that the general mechanisms of cellularization in S. arctica are likely conserved within ichthyosporeans.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that many cellularization genes emerged at the onset of ichthyosporeans

claim: Cellularization in ichthyosporeans requires both regulatory pathways conserved with animals, as well as regulatory pathways that evolved independently in ichthyosporeans.
source: Altogether, our results argue that cellularization in ichthyosporeans requires both regulatory pathways conserved with animals, as well as regulatory pathways that evolved independently in ichthyosporeans.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the transcriptomic and phylostratigraphic analyses

claim: LincRNAs that are remarkably conserved among ichthyosporeans and show high expression levels may be part of regulatory pathways that evolved independently in ichthyosporeans.
source: The later may include lincRNAs that we found to be remarkably conserved among ichthyosporeans and show high expression levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lincRNA conservation and expression data

claim: The conserved cell-cell adhesion and cell-matrix adhesion pathways are transcriptionally upregulated during cellularization concomitantly with the formation of polarized layer of cells.
source: Among pathways transcriptionally upregulated during cellularization are the conserved cell-cell adhesion and cell-matrix adhesion pathways, which occur concomitantly with the formation of polarized layer of cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data

claim: Cell-cell adhesion and cell-matrix adhesion pathways are hallmarks of epithelial tissues in animals.
source: These pathways are hallmarks of epithelial tissues in animals (Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014

claim: The epithelium is the first tissue that is established during embryogenesis and perhaps the first that emerged in evolution, thus representing the basic form of multicellular organization in animals.
source: The epithelium is the first tissue that is established during embryogenesis and perhaps the first that emerged in evolution, thus representing the basic form of multicellular organization in animals (Brunet and King, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Brunet and King, 2017

claim: Epithelia are found in all animal lineages, including sponges.
source: Epithelia are found in all animal lineages, including sponges (Leys et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leys et al., 2009

claim: The origin of epithelial structures predates the origin of animals, as a polarized non-cadherin-based epithelium-like structure, regulated by alpha and beta catenins, is also present in the slime mold Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: It has previously been suggested that the origin of epithelial structures predates the origin of animals, as a polarized non-cadherin-based epithelium-like structure, regulated by alpha and beta catenins, is also present in the slime mold Dictyostelium discoideum (Dickinson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dickinson et al., 2011

claim: Cellularization in S. arctica generates a transient epithelium-like layer of cells.
source: Based on this indirect evidence from transcriptomics, we hypothesize that cellularization in S. arctica generates a transient epithelium-like layer of cells, lending support to the hypothesis that the origin of epithelial tissues predates the origin of animals (Dickinson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on transcriptomic data and citation to Dickinson et al., 2012

claim: Unlike the epithelium formation in social amoebae, which originates through aggregation, ichthyosporean epithelium is generated clonally, such as in animals.
source: However, unlike the epithelium formation in social amoebae, which originates through aggregation (Bonner, 1998), ichthyosporean epithelium is generated clonally, such as in animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with social amoebae and citation to Bonner, 1998

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, cellularization is accomplished through plasma membrane invaginations around equally spaced, cortically positioned nuclei.
source: In contrast, in a model animal coenocyte, the syncytial blastoderm of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, cellularization is accomplished through plasma membrane invaginations around equally spaced, cortically positioned nuclei (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014; Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014; Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002

claim: Cellularization in Drosophila relies on extensive membrane remodeling regulated by zygotically transcribed genes and driven by microtubules and a contractile actomyosin network.
source: This process relies on extensive membrane remodeling (Lecuit, 2004; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Figard et al., 2016) regulated by zygotically transcribed genes (Schweisguth et al., 1990; Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993; Postner and Wieschaus, 1994; Hunter and Wieschaus, 2000; Lecuit et al., 2002) and driven by microtubules and a contractile actomyosin network (Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations: Lecuit, 2004; Sokac and Wieschaus, 2008; Figard et al., 2016; Schweisguth et al., 1990; Schejter and Wieschaus, 1993; Postner and Wieschaus, 1994; Hunter and Wieschaus, 2000; Lecuit et al., 2002; Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002

claim: Cellularization in Drosophila depends on several actin nucleators, such as the Arp2/3 complex and formins.
source: It depends on several actin nucleators, such as the Arp2/3 complex (Stevenson et al., 2002) and formins (Afshar et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stevenson et al., 2002 and Afshar et al., 2000

claim: Cellularization in Drosophila requires multiple actin-binding proteins, including myosin II, septins, cofilin and profilin.
source: It also requires multiple actin-binding proteins, including myosin II (Royou et al., 2002), which mediates actin cross-linking and contractility, as well as septins (Adam et al., 2000; Cooper and Kiehart, 1996), cofilin (Gunsalus et al., 1995) and profilin (Giansanti et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Royou et al., 2002; Adam et al., 2000; Cooper and Kiehart, 1996; Gunsalus et al., 1995; Giansanti et al., 1998

claim: Cellularization in Drosophila depends on cell-cell adhesion proteins including cadherin, and alpha- and beta-catenin.
source: In addition, it depends on cell-cell adhesion proteins including cadherin, and alpha- and beta-catenin (Hunter and Wieschaus, 2000; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hunter and Wieschaus, 2000; Wang et al., 2004

claim: Coordinated cellularization in Drosophila results in the formation of a single layer of polarized epithelial tissue, also known as cellular blastoderm.
source: This coordinated cellularization results in the formation of a single layer of polarized epithelial tissue, also known as cellular blastoderm (Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mazumdar and Mazumdar, 2002

claim: Actomyosin-dependent cellularization is common in early insect embryos and also commonly observed in germline development of many animals.
source: This actomyosin-dependent cellularization is common in early insect embryos and also commonly observed in germline development of many animals (Haglund et al., 2011), such as the nematode C. elegans (Priti et al., 2018), however, whether this mechanism of cellularization is found outside animals, remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haglund et al., 2011 and Priti et al., 2018

claim: During endosperm development in most flowering plants, coenocytes cellularize through cell wall formation around individual nuclei, forming a peripheral layer of cells surrounding a central vacuole.
source: During endosperm development in most flowering plants, coenocytes cellularize through cell wall formation around individual nuclei, forming a peripheral layer of cells surrounding a central vacuole (Hehenberger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hehenberger et al., 2012

claim: Plant coenocyte cellularization is coordinated by the radial microtubule system and is dependent on several microtubule-associated proteins.
source: This is coordinated by the radial microtubule system and is dependent on several microtubule-associated proteins (Pignocchi et al., 2009; Sørensen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pignocchi et al., 2009; Sørensen et al., 2002

claim: In apicomplexan parasites, cytokinesis of multinucleate schizonts occurs by budding, which is driven by a polarized microtubule scaffold.
source: In apicomplexan parasites, cytokinesis of multinucleate schizonts occurs by budding, which is driven by a polarized microtubule scaffold (Francia and Striepen, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Francia and Striepen, 2014
